body:
Fixes #5985.

When an allocation failed while `json::parse()` built an object or array member, the result was destroyed with a member whose type said *object*/*array* but whose pointer was null, so the destructor dereferenced it instead of the `std::bad_alloc` reaching the caller. Introduced by #5882 (not in any release).

### Cause and fix

`json_sax_dom_parser::set_member()` placement-news the new value over the null member it inserted for the key. `basic_json(value_t)` writes `m_type` before the allocation of `m_value`, so a throwing allocation left the member half-overwritten. Now a value whose construction can throw (a string, a binary value or a container) is created in a local first and placement-new'd into the member by move (the move constructor is `noexcept`), so a failed allocation never touches the member. A value that is nothrow-constructible (null, boolean, numbers) is still constructed in place, as before, so it pays no extra move; the choice is made at compile time with `std::is_nothrow_constructible`. This also covers `ordered_json`, `JSON_DIAGNOSTICS` and `sax_parse()` with `detail::json_sax_dom_parser` into an existing value (same code). The callback parser and the binary parsers assign a temporary and were not affected.

### Tests

`tests/src/unit-allocator.cpp`: "parse() survives a failing allocation at every point (#5985)" fails allocation k = 1, 2, … with a counting allocator (checks for a clean `std::bad_alloc` and no leak) for `json`, `ordered_json`, the callback parser (keep-all and filtering) and `sax_parse()` into an existing value. On develop it crashes under UBSan (`json.hpp:912: reference binding to null pointer`); with the fix it passes, also with `JSON_DIAGNOSTICS=1`. The issue's reproducer now runs to `no throw at k=14: done`. Full `ctest` with ASan+UBSan: 188/188.

### Performance

The alternative (setting `m_type` after the allocation in `data(value_t)`) was prototyped too; both were measured against develop with an A/B harness (Mac instruction counts, DOM parse, `json` and `ordered_json`). The chosen fix is at or below develop on all large inputs (twitter 0.996, citm 0.999, canada 0.999, update-center 0.993–0.999, random 0.994–0.996); the alternative was up to +0.8 %. Small inputs (< 1e8 instructions) stay within their ±2 % noise.

These numbers were measured before scalars went back to in-place construction (review follow-up, 4809610d60). That change only removes work from the scalar path, and it has not been re-measured.

### Public API

No breaking changes.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

comments.body:
### Performance check

**No measurable impact.** This touches the hottest part of DOM parsing (creating every new object member), so I checked it closely.

- **Generated code** (clang, arm64): `json_sax_dom_parser::store<...>()` changes for every value type. For scalar members, the move adds one store instruction: the zeroing of the slot is split into separate stores. For strings and containers (`store<value_t>`, `store<string_t>`), the functions are actually **one 16-byte block shorter**. The temporary's destructor apparently folds away, since the moved-from value is known to be null. Nothing else changes.
- **Instruction counts**:

| case | clang/arm64 PR/base | GCC/x86-64 (callgrind, exact) PR/base |
|---|---:|---:|
| parse twitter | 0.9976 | 1.00081 |
| parse citm_catalog | 0.9986 | 1.00004 |
| parse canada | 0.9973 | 1.00000 |
| parse twitter from `std::istream` | 0.9975 | 1.00066 |
| parse twitter with callback | 0.9990 | 1.00000 |

  The worst case is GCC on twitter at +0.08 % (19k instructions out of 23.2M per parse). That is well under the 1 % threshold. On clang every row is within noise. The other 33 rows are also within noise.

<details><summary>Method</summary>

- PR head vs. its base (merge base), both compiled into one binary (namespaces renamed per copy) with the same workload: DOM parse (string, stream, callback), copy/destroy, `==`/`<`, iteration, `dump()`, msgpack/UBJSON/BJData read and write, `json_document` parse/`dump()`/`==`/`get<std::int64_t>()` on twitter, citm_catalog, canada and small_signed_ints.
- **Generated code**: both variants disassembled (Apple clang 21, `-O3`, arm64), names and addresses masked, compared function by function.
- **Instruction counts**: Apple M1 Max, instructions retired per repetition (minimum of 3 runs, setup subtracted). Rows whose machine code is identical vary by about ±0.4 %, which is the noise floor. Where a hot path changes, also GCC 13.3 `-O3` on x86-64 under callgrind, which gives exact counts (built with `-falign-functions=64 -falign-loops=64` unless a row says otherwise).
</details>

---
*Written by Claude Code on behalf of @nlohmann.*

linked_issues.title: parse() crashes in the destructor instead of propagating std::bad_alloc (the DOM parser leaves a half-constructed member)

review_comments.body: astyle (probably the &&, not sure that can be fixed)
You don't know it's a scalar, just that it's `nothrow_constructible`.

Fixed in f00fe043f0: it was the `&&`. Since `Value` is a forwarding-reference parameter, `std::is_nothrow_constructible<BasicJsonType, Value>` asks the same question as `Value &&` (`Value` is `T` for an rvalue and `T&` for an lvalue), and astyle leaves that spelling alone.

*(Written by Claude Code on behalf of @nlohmann.)*

Right, the overload is selected by `std::is_nothrow_constructible`, not by the value being a scalar. Fixed in f00fe043f0: the comments now say "constructing the value cannot throw (a number, a boolean)" and "constructing the value can throw (a container, a string)". No behaviour change.

*(Written by Claude Code on behalf of @nlohmann.)*

I was assuming the possibility that there are custom containers or strings that are nothrow constructible, but I'm not sure how likely that is.  I suppose they could use a custom arena that is guaranteed to never throw.

Agreed, that case works: the trait is the whole criterion, so a custom string or container whose construction is declared `noexcept` (an arena that cannot fail, say) takes the in-place path, and that is correct because there is no interrupted constructor to worry about. For the default types it is only the numbers and booleans (I checked: `std::string`, `array_t` and `object_t` all report `false`). If such a type claimed `noexcept` and threw anyway, the program would already terminate in its constructor, whichever way the member is placed. The "(a number, a boolean)" in the comment is only the usual examples; I can make it "for example" if you think it reads as the condition.

*(Written by Claude Code on behalf of @nlohmann.)*

Yes, I think "for example" would help there, to make it clear that these aren't trying to detect "primitives" vs "containers" but "potentially throwing" and "can't throw", so that it's okay if a custom non-throwing container gets into the first one.  Don't want someone to think that they might need a check to push containers to the second one, or even worse, push a custom number class to the first one when it is not nothrow constructible.

Right, that is the distinction I want the comments to carry: "may throw" versus "cannot throw", decided by `std::is_nothrow_constructible`, not by primitive versus container. Done in 2906d8d44c: both comments now say "for example", so a custom non-throwing container landing in the first overload is expected, and nobody needs a check to route anything.

*(Written by Claude Code on behalf of @nlohmann.)*

title: parse(): propagate std::bad_alloc instead of crashing on a half-constructed member
